newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian blue chips higher, Zagrebacka seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Croatian blue chips higher, Zagrebacka seen rising.

text.p: Croatian stocks were mostly higher in a livelier trade on Tuesday, with blue chips posting gains on higher volumes.
Traders predicted Zagrebacka Banka to continue rising on good ratings and business results released earlier today.
Zagrebacka, the leading Croatian commercial bank, closed at 1,850 kuna ($304) -- 50 up from last Friday -- with 1,900 shares changing hands.
But news that IBCA, the European credit rating agency, assigned it a long-term rating of BBB- and a short term of A3 came too late in the day to influence the trading at the Zagreb bourse.

The bank also released its 1996 business results, saying the group's pre-tax profit rose to 349 million kuna, compared to a 143 million loss a year earlier. The parent bank's pre-tax profit rose to 266 million kuna from 162 million in 1995.
"The results are 30 to 40 percent better than expected, but they came in just after closing of the bourse, so they did not affect the trading," Josko Milisa of I.C.F brokerage told Reuters.
"But I expect the price tomorrow to go up above 1,900 kuna," he added.
In London, Zagrebacka's 1/10 Global Depository Receipts were traded at up to $32.75 after opening at $31.375, but edged down to $32.5 in the afternoon.
Another market heavyweight, drug firm Pliva, did also well, gaining 10.5 kuna to close at 450.5, on the day's record volume of 3,654 shares.
Growing interest in Pliva is spurred by expectations of good 1996 business results to be released by the end of the month.
But the expected bull run was slow in coming ahead of the country-wide local elections, scheduled for next weekend, Milisa said.

"The most important thing is to see how it would go in Eastern Slavonia," he said, referring to a majority-Serb area supposed to come back under Zagreb's rule in July, where Serbs are to take a part in the poll for the first time since their 1991 rebellion against Croatian independence.
"Any disturbances would affect the market in the negative sense," he said.
Chocolate maker Kras gained 5 kuna to close on 415 on small volume, while food producer Podravka has traded heavily -- selling 3,116 shares -- gaining one kuna to 299.
"I suppose these levels are low enough that some investors were attracted regardless of the elections," Milisa said.
He also saw some growing potential in tourist shares, which were being traded now on the bottom of the range, but their recovery will have to wait until the next week.
"The ask and bid are coming closer together on some of those shares, and that is a good sign," Milisa said.
He singled out Istraturist, which inched up 10 kuna to 190 on volume of 279 shares on Tuesday.
The volume almost tripled to 11,142 shares from 4,104 on Friday, while the turnover more than doubled to 6.7 million kuna from 2.7 million. Of 13 active issues six were up, two down and five flat.
Biggest decliner hotelier Riviera Porec lost nine kuna to 145 on volume of 110 shares. ($ = 6.091 Croatian Kuna)
